li.a: L'Unità, 7 June 1997, page 5: the arrest of Pietro Aglieri and a profile of the boss
Die Welt, 8 June 1997: Er betete zum Schutzpatron der Polizei
Corriere della Sera, 14 February 1999 (archived copy): Via D'Amelio, sette ergastoli
19luglio1992.com, 12 November 2009: Alfonso Sabella, un giudice stritolato dalla Trattativa
Il Fatto Quotidiano, 15 December 2014: Borsellino quater, depone il boss Aglieri
Progetto San Francesco: Borsellino quater, reports of Aglieri's testimony of 15 December 2014
Die Zeit, 20 April 2006: Gottvater hinter Gittern

content.p: Pietro Aglieri was, for years, the Sicilian mafia boss that Italian newspapers could describe only in contradictions. He was a convicted man with a seminary diploma, an elegant dresser who kept a tiny chapel in his hideout, and a fugitive some rumours placed in Brazil who was in fact living close to Palermo. On Friday 6 June 1997, police surrounded one of his refuges near Bagheria and took him in a raid that lasted about two minutes. Italy's head of state telegraphed his congratulations. Die Welt reported that a white sheet hung from a balcony in the centre of Palermo with a single word on it: "Grazie".

The rest of Aglieri's story is a long argument about what he was and what he wanted. He is serving life sentences, among them the one for the bombing in Via D'Amelio in July 1992 that killed anti-mafia magistrate Paolo Borsellino and the five police officers guarding him. He has never become a state witness. Yet from his prison cell he became associated with the idea, floated in the early 2000s, that jailed bosses might "dissociate" from Cosa Nostra in return for easier terms. In December 2014, in a courtroom in Caltanissetta, he finally answered questions about all of it, in his own words, without ever once agreeing that the organisation existed.

L'Unità, in a profile printed the morning after the arrest, built the boss's life from the accounts of informers and investigators. Aglieri was born to Vincenzo Aglieri and Giuseppa Di Maio and came from the Guadagna district of Palermo, where, the paper wrote, his grandfather had been a man of respect in the mafia sense who liked to ride through the streets in a horse-drawn calesse, dressed entirely in white with an elegant panama hat. The grandson inherited the manners, and the nickname "u signurinu" followed, for his passion for fine clothes.

The paper reported that he had earned a classical school-leaving diploma at the seminary attached to the Palermo archdiocese, under a monsignor described as vicar to Cardinal Pappalardo, and that he had done military service with the Folgore paratroopers, where some remembered him for his daring and cold blood. Die Welt gave a different seminary: it wrote that he finished school at the priests' seminary in Monreale. The two accounts agree that his education was religious and unusually thorough for a man in his trade.

His rise, according to L'Unità, was already visible to the police in 1983. When he was 24, the paper wrote, a judge named Giovanni Falcone and Falcone's close colleague Ninni Cassarà, then head of the flying squad, read his name in an anonymous tip that said to keep an eye on him because he was very young but would go far. The paper credited an old boss, Pietro Lo Jacono, with his early training. The killing of Bontade and his wife, it said, won Aglieri the favour of Totò Riina, who according to the informer Pino Marchese made him head of the Santa Maria di Gesù district.

The same profile attributed to informers a string of crimes. Francesco Marino Mannoia, a former right-hand man of Bontade, described the killing of an elderly man, Benedetto Grado, who was about eighty and walked with a stick; L'Unità wrote that Aglieri had already received a life sentence for it. It also described the double murder of Giovanni Bontade and his wife Francesca Citarda, carried out by killers who had entered their home disguised as police officers and were offered coffee by the couple. L'Unità listed that case among the crimes Aglieri was accused of, which is a looser claim than a conviction. The paper added that, in the view of informers, his part in the 1992 massacres at Capaci and Via D'Amelio was not "operational" but one of direction.

L'Unità placed Aglieri at the centre of the realignment inside Cosa Nostra after Riina's arrest in January 1993. L'Unità called him a two-faced figure. On one side, it said, he had turned off the switch of the escalation against the state; on the other he had set himself up as leader of the Palermo bosses, recruiting men who had fled the first mafia war of the mid-1980s and who had never given up the idea of revenge on Riina and his Corleone faction.

The informer Salvatore Cancemi told investigators that Bernardo Provenzano had given Aglieri the go-ahead for an anti-Corleonese cartel, according to the paper. Another, Salvatore Barbagallo, described Cosa Nostra as split into two camps by 1994: one around Leoluca Bagarella and Giovanni Brusca, the other around Aglieri, who was said to be gathering the "losers" for an offensive against the Corleonesi. L'Unità reported that dozens of killings between November 1994 and the spring of 1995, in and around Palermo, were read by investigators as confirmation of Barbagallo's description. It also reported that investigators had come to suspect Aglieri's hand behind a plan to kill Riina's young son Giovanni.

The same piece described Provenzano as Aglieri's "spiritual father" and, in its words, the last great number one still in circulation. Aglieri's role, in the paper's phrase, was to give Cosa Nostra a "facelift" for the year 2000: to put the Kalashnikov away, restore calm and reopen contacts with parts of the institutions.

The legends about where he was only added to the myth. L'Unità recalled a claim in May 1996 by a judge named Walter Fanganiello, that Aglieri might be in Brazil running a drug-transit and money-laundering operation. Italian officials, among them the deputy head of the anti-mafia agency Dia, were sceptical: they said every major Cosa Nostra fugitive had always been found in Sicily. Other stories placed him on a cruise ship, or at a 1994 summit in Marseille; the paper called the second of these a big hoax.
content.h2: Six June 1997: the raid at Fondo Marino
content.p: The operation was run by the Palermo prosecutors' office and the city's flying squad. L'Unità reported that the refuge, in the Fondo Marino area between Bagheria and Ficarazzi, had been identified three days earlier, after investigations that had lasted months. Officers filmed and photographed the people coming and going, and compared the images on a computer with old police photographs of Aglieri; they matched in many points, but the police were not yet sure. The paper reported that the encirclement lasted seventy-two hours.

The assault came at a quarter past ten on the Friday. Roughly three hundred officers under flying-squad chief Luigi Savina took part, and about a hundred climbed the three-metre wall around a property that looked like a store for lemons and oranges. Inside there were two rooms, a stable, a courtyard and a small chapel with benches, sacred images and a Madonna. They fired three flash-bang devices and aimed weapons at three men: Aglieri, his squad leader Giuseppe La Mattina and his adviser Natale Gambino. None of them was armed. Aglieri did not resist, did not speak and let himself be handcuffed. Savina said the police had the impression the chapel was a place for mafia initiation and oaths.

The sources disagree over what led the police there. Die Welt reported that the two-month operation was triggered by the informer Giovanni Brusca, who had been in prison since 1996 and gave the decisive tip. L'Unità wrote that a rumour that Brusca had recognised Aglieri from a photograph was denied and had not been confirmed that anyone had been shown the photograph. The official line, from prosecutor Alfonso Sabella, was that the arrest came from tailing suspects and from bugging of rooms and telephones, though the paper wrote that this did not remove the suspicion that someone Aglieri knew and trusted had set the operation in motion.

Both newspapers described the same detail: the boss's devotion. Die Welt said police found books by Edith Stein and Kierkegaard, a small altar dedicated to Saint Michael the Archangel, patron saint of the police, and about a hundred holy cards. He wore a gold chain and crucifix. According to newspaper reports quoted by Die Welt, which the judicial authorities had not confirmed, he prayed standing for two hours in his cell, and told a judge he repented before God but not before men. That sentence is attributed to him as a report, not as a verified quotation.

The reaction was mixed with caution. Palermo's chief prosecutor Giancarlo Caselli said, according to Die Welt, that the arrest was a great success but that the mafia was far from beaten, and that Italy must not relax. The paper added that 13 "superbosses" were still on the wanted list. Die Welt added that the 34-year-old Sabella, who it said had led the arrest, gloomily predicted that there would soon be deaths again, perhaps his own. Palermo's police commissioner, Antonio Manganelli, told L'Unità that the arrest showed the state was serious.
content.h2: The courts: Via D'Amelio and its false trail
content.p: At the time of his arrest, according to Die Welt, Aglieri had already been sentenced in his absence to life for the murder of Judge Scopelliti, and to twelve years for mafia membership and drug trafficking. The weightier case came from Via D'Amelio.

The first trial for the bombing had opened on 24 October 1994 and ended with life sentences for three men. By the time of the 1999 appeal verdict, Corriere della Sera reported, the case had collapsed in part: on 23 January 1999 the appeal court acquitted Pietro Scotto and Giuseppe Orofino and upheld life only for Salvatore Profeta. The prosecution's star witness, the former informer Vincenzo Scarantino, had retracted everything and received 18 years, which became final.

The second trial, the "Borsellino bis", began in 1997 with 18 defendants, including Riina and Aglieri, accused of ordering the massacre of 19 July 1992. Its verdict came on 13 February 1999, after 12 days of deliberation. The court sentenced seven men to life: Riina, Aglieri, Salvatore Biondino, Carlo Greco, Giuseppe Graviano, Gaetano Scotto and Francesco Tagliavia. Eight "picciotti" were acquitted of the massacre itself but convicted of mafia association, with sentences of 8 to 10 years. Among those acquitted of the massacre were Natale Gambino and Giuseppe La Mattina, the two men arrested with Aglieri. Corriere's correspondent, Felice Cavallaro, wrote that the court had accepted the "objective responsibility" of the leadership, the so-called Buscetta theorem, while questioning the lesser defendants. A third trial, the "ter", involving 26 further bosses, was running in parallel.
content.h2: Dissociation: a boss who says he never asked for it
content.p: From 2000 Aglieri's name resurfaced in an argument in Rome and Palermo, set out by Alfonso Sabella, who had by then moved from the Palermo prosecutors to the prison administration. In an account published on 19luglio1992.com, Sabella said that in May 2000 the director of the prison administration, Caselli, showed him a letter from Justice Minister Piero Fassino asking for an opinion on investigative interviews held by the national anti-mafia prosecutor Pier Luigi Vigna with four jailed bosses: Aglieri, Giuseppe "Piddu" Madonia, Salvatore Buscemi and Giuseppe Farinella. According to Sabella, the four said they were willing to dissociate publicly from Cosa Nostra at no cost, admitting responsibility for crimes for which they had already been sentenced and accusing no one. He wrote that Aglieri first asked, on behalf of the others, to meet other jailed bosses who were also willing, among them Nitto Santapaola, Salvo Madonia, Carlo Greco and Pippo Calò.

Sabella argued that the four were the "ideologues" of the plan, that they belonged to Provenzano's area, and that dissociation would have brought them the end of "41 bis" and large cuts to life sentences. He said he opposed it. In his telling, in the autumn of 2001 he raised an alarm after prison administrators asked for approval for Biondino to work as a cleaner, a job that would have given him free access to the cells of Aglieri, Farinella, Madonia and Buscemi, and that the alarm cost him his office on 5 December 2001 when his new chief, Giovanni Tinebra, abolished it. These are Sabella's claims, published in his own words; Tinebra's reasons are not given on the page.

Aglieri's own account, given in court, was different. Il Fatto Quotidiano and Progetto San Francesco, reporting from the Caltanissetta hearing on 15 December 2014, quoted him saying he had a meeting in prison with Vigna and told him he had nothing to dissociate from or repent. When Vigna asked what could be done for the land they came from, Aglieri said he replied that the only possibility was that from that moment each person could reflect and stop acting against the state. It was not a negotiation or a dissociation, he said, but a "desistenza", a word borrowed from the law on terrorism. He added that he never asked for the removal of "41 bis", but spoke of prison benefits for individual detainees, and that after his arrest he had been told that extortion in his area of influence had increased, which he said went against his way of thinking. Asked by prosecutor Nico Gozzo whether he meant stopping the association called Cosa Nostra, he answered that whether the association existed or not, all of them had been convicted of that crime and so had to stop the crime charged. In the paper's words, a rare example of pure mafia pragmatism.
content.h2: December 2014: the boss on the witness stand
content.p: The setting was the Borsellino quater trial in Caltanissetta, opened after the informer Gaspare Spatuzza overturned the version of events told by Scarantino. Il Fatto Quotidiano described Aglieri as someone who was not a state witness, had never repented, had never admitted that Cosa Nostra existed or that he belonged to it, and was serving a life sentence as both instigator and perpetrator of the Via D'Amelio massacre. Scarantino had named him as the man who pressed the remote control. Two years earlier he had agreed to answer prosecutors' questions; in December 2014, by video link from Rebibbia prison, he agreed for the first time to testify at trial, as an "assisted witness".

He knew Scarantino, he said, as a neighbour in Guadagna whom he saw almost daily, and he excluded that he would have trusted such a man with any important task. When Scarantino left a protected location and went home, Aglieri said, the bosses were told and he said that nobody should touch him, because he was only a poor devil caught in something bigger. He said Scarantino's family reported pressure on him in custody, and that Arnaldo La Barbera, then head of the Palermo flying squad, acted in bad faith. He added that he had known from the start that Scarantino had nothing to do with the theft of the 126 car, after checks, and that he suspected evidence was being built against the bosses.

Aglieri contradicted the informer Antonino Giuffrè, who had said that in 1993 Aglieri or his deputy Carlo Greco asked him to erase the trace of Scarantino's presence at a hotel in Trabia on the day of the massacre, with Provenzano reportedly calling Scarantino a man who would ruin them all. Aglieri said the bosses had checked, found no sign of Scarantino at the hotel and thought it was in their interest that he be shown to have been there. Il Fatto Quotidiano reported that he invoked the right not to answer in two places: when asked about his personal relations with Riina, and when a lawyer asked whether he had attended meetings to exchange Christmas greetings. The reference, the paper explained, was to summits in the winter of 1991 in a farmhouse near Enna, where Cosa Nostra's strategy was set in case the Maxi Trial sentences were confirmed. His curt reply, as quoted: he had not attended meetings to exchange Christmas greetings, nor Easter greetings.

The pages consulted show Aglieri under a life sentence as of 2014, convicted for Via D'Amelio and yet testifying in a trial built on the collapse of Scarantino's version. The Borsellino bis verdict named him a "mandante", an instigator; in 2014 Il Fatto Quotidiano wrote that he stood definitively convicted as both instigator and perpetrator, after Scarantino had named him as the man who pressed the remote control. Whether the later trials changed his sentence is not given in the pages consulted. Nor do they settle who tipped off the police in 1997, whether he truly sought dissociation, or what he meant by the "desistenza" he described to Vigna. Die Zeit, writing in 2006 about the arrest of Provenzano, called him the leading mind of a new generation of mafiosi.
